'I said I'm busy.'

I'm Farhan. In my third year of college in Aligarh, Naveen from the photography club asked if I wanted to go for a sunset walk by the old fort and get chai after. Just the two of us. He said it shyly, which I remember now.

I said no. I said I had a project. The truth is I'd already watched the whole evening in my head: long silences, me talking too much about lenses, Naveen checking his phone, both of us relieved when it ended. I knew it would be awkward, so why go and be disappointed?

The relief was immediate. I spent that evening in my room, safe.

But the photos from that walk, which he posted later with a group, were beautiful. And I kept doing it that whole year. No to the trip, no to the dinner. Each no felt safe. My world just got a little smaller every time.

qa.q: Where did Naveen invite Farhan to go?
qa.a: For a sunset walk by the old fort and chai after.

qa.q: Why did saying no bring Farhan relief straight away?
qa.a: Declining meant Farhan couldn't be disappointed or embarrassed by an evening that already seemed sure to go badly. The prediction protected Farhan from risk, so turning it down felt safe.

qa.q: What could Farhan try the next time an invitation seems sure to go badly?
qa.a: Treat the prediction as a guess and say yes to a short version, like chai only, then compare what actually happens with the forecast. Small tests would show whether that certainty is right.

qa.q: How might Naveen have felt after asking shyly and hearing about a project?
qa.a: Naveen may have felt disappointed or unsure whether Farhan was interested at all. Having taken a risk to ask, Naveen might hesitate to ask again.

grounding: A young adult declines an invitation out of certainty that the evening will be awkward, gaining relief while life slowly narrows.

passage:
Counselling cell note, second visit

Uma, 20, came back today. Last week she mentioned that a classmate, Ravi, had asked her to dinner on Saturday. Today she told me she had said no.

I asked why. She said, without pausing, "It would have been awkward. I'd run out of things to say by the soup. He'd realise I'm boring. I'd come home embarrassed. So I saved us both."

She said it with a small smile, as if describing something that had already happened. When I asked how she felt on Saturday night, she said, "Safe. And a bit lonely." Then she said this was the third invitation she has turned down this term.

I pointed out, gently, that none of those evenings had happened, yet each had been graded as a failure.

Next step: Uma agreed to write down her prediction before the next invitation, go for a short time, and bring both to our next session. Our next meeting is on the 14th.

— Jaya, counsellor

qa.q: How many invitations has Uma turned down this term?
qa.a: This is the third invitation she has turned down this term.

qa.q: What does Uma's answer "Safe. And a bit lonely" reveal about how she felt?
qa.a: It shows her mixed feelings: the prediction spared her from possible embarrassment, but it also left her missing out. Staying safe came with a cost she could feel.

qa.q: Why is the plan Jaya and Uma made a good way to test her prediction?
qa.a: Writing the forecast down and then going for a short time lets Uma compare what she expected with what actually happens. Real evidence can loosen a prediction that feels like knowledge.

qa.q: How might Ravi see Uma's no, without knowing her reasons?
qa.a: Ravi might think Uma isn't interested in him, or feel a bit rejected. Ravi has no way of knowing that she was protecting herself from a dinner she'd already imagined going badly.

grounding: A counsellor notes a young woman who turns down invitations because she is sure they will be awkward, protecting herself while her life narrows.
